subject: biology
title: Human Physiology Adventure 2: Blood, circulation, and gas exchange
welcome_lead: Today you'll pump blood through the double circulation and exchange gases.
meta_desc: Biology — heart, double circulation, haemoglobin, Bohr shift, alveoli.
final_note: You learned the heart drives double circulation, haemoglobin shows sigmoid O₂ dissociation, the Bohr shift releases O₂ in active tissue, and alveoli maximise gas exchange.

concepts.def: Curve shifts right with high CO₂

walkthroughs.body_html:
Mammals have double circulation: pulmonary (heart-lungs-heart) and systemic (heart-body-heart).

Right atrium → right ventricle → pulmonary artery → lungs → pulmonary vein → left atrium → left ventricle → aorta.

The SA node sets pace (~70 bpm), signal passes via AV node to ventricles. Resting cardiac output ≈ 5 L/min.

Hb has 4 subunits, each binding O₂ cooperatively → sigmoid dissociation curve.

P50 ≈ 3.5 kPa (50% saturated). In high CO₂ (active muscle), curve shifts right — the Bohr shift — releasing more O₂ where needed.

Fetal Hb sits left of adult — higher affinity, pulling O₂ from maternal blood across placenta.

~300 million alveoli, total SA ~70 m². Adaptations:

- Thin epithelium (one cell thick).
- Rich capillary network.
- Surfactant prevents collapse.
- Ventilation maintains gradient.

Fick's law: rate ∝ SA × Δc / thickness.

Why are food chains usually limited to about 4 or 5 trophic levels?
options: There aren't enough types of animals to fill more trophic levels.
Larger animals always eat the next ones up, and there aren't enough giant animals.
Only ~10 percent of energy is transferred between trophic levels; eventually too little energy remains to support another level.
